title: Inscribe Alternatives: Why Buyers Look Elsewhere and Who Fits
summary: Six Inscribe alternatives, sorted by what a buyer needs: work after the flag, document mix, data terms, pricing and how edits get caught.
body_markdown:
**TL;DR:** Inscribe is a serious document fraud platform with a real agentic layer, so the useful question is what a buyer needs that it was not built around. Five things separate the alternatives: the case work after the flag, a document mix beyond US lending, data terms, pricing visibility, and how well edited real files get caught. Inscribe's own 2026 report flagged about 6 percent of documents, roughly 1 in 16, so whichever tool you pick, the check itself stays necessary.


Sphinx wrote this list, and it sells one of the products on it. The order is an order of fit for a team reconsidering Inscribe, based on each vendor's public pages, and it does not rank detection accuracy.


## What Inscribe does well, and where it has moved


Inscribe is a document fraud detection platform for banks, credit unions, fintechs and lenders, founded in 2017 and built around the files that move money: bank statements, pay stubs, tax forms and business documents. Its pages describe forensic, network, semantic and perceptual detection, with custom signals and public data enrichment on top. Each result carries a risk level and a plain-language explanation, which is more than a bare score. Inscribe also publishes customer results, including a 90 percent cut in manual document review time, and it holds SOC 2 and ISO 27001.


The move toward AI analysts is real. Inscribe announced AI Risk Agents in 2024, then an AI Fraud Analyst that checks documents, verifies applicant details through database and web research, and writes an auditable risk report in about 90 seconds. Today it calls itself an agentic document fraud platform. The 2026 releases added an in-product Assistant that answers questions about a flagged file, Custom Transaction Insights with backtesting, a configurable Decision Engine, and an integration that returns findings into Taktile's decision workflows.


Read closely, those pages aim the agent at one thing: the documents in an application, and the people and businesses behind them. That focus is the product's strength. It also explains most of the reasons below.


## Five reasons an Inscribe buyer starts looking


Generic best-of lists compare feature grids. Someone already evaluating or running Inscribe usually has a narrower problem, and it tends to be one of these.


### The backlog sits after the flag


Inscribe clears low-risk files and sends flagged ones to a queue with the evidence assembled. For an underwriter, that is close to the end of the job. For a KYB or EDD analyst, the document finding is one step in a case that still needs registry checks, ownership research, screening hits and a written note in the case manager. A suspected forgery can also turn into a reporting question:[FinCEN's November 2024 alert](https://www.fincen.gov/news/news-releases/fincen-issues-alert-fraud-schemes-involving-deepfake-media-targeting-financial) reported a rise in suspicious activity reports describing deepfake media, particularly fraudulent identity documents. A compliance team whose bottleneck is that whole case looks for something that works the case, and a better detector would not touch it.


### The document mix drifted away from US lending


Inscribe's own vendor comparison describes its buyers as US banks, credit unions, fintechs and lenders, and it describes its network the same way. That is a fine center of gravity for US income documents. A payments company onboarding businesses across several countries sees a different pile: foreign registry extracts, certificates of incumbency, translated bank letters. Inscribe does accept business filings, so nobody should assume a gap. Test your own[KYB document packs](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/kyb-document-fraud-detection) and see whether the signals hold up on them.


### The network is the strength, and also the contract question


Inscribe's CEO has said its detection advantage comes from measuring documents against a large network. Comparing files against millions of applications does catch recycled templates. The trade-off appears in the paperwork. Inscribe's public terms allow customer data to be used to improve its services, including training models, and its pages also describe configurable retention and say sensitive data is not shared with external model providers. Negotiated agreements may differ, so read yours, and ask every vendor on this list the same data questions.[The 2023 interagency guidance on third-party relationships](https://www.fdic.gov/news/financial-institution-letters/2023/fil23029.html) is plain that using a vendor does not reduce a bank's own responsibility, and some security teams will want a narrower license than the public default. Others will happily trade data for network coverage.


### Procurement wants a number before the pilot


Inscribe sells Base and Premium plans at custom prices based on volume and features, with a complimentary four-week pilot on your own sample. The pilot is thorough and costs nothing in fees. It also takes a month and a sales cycle, which is a lot for a team that needs a budget figure this quarter or checks a few hundred files a month.


### Edited real files are the hard class


Inscribe's report says AI-generated documents made up less than 5 percent of the fraud it detected in 2025, and a mid-2026 update puts template fraud at two to three times the volume of AI-generated fraud. The same update says, "AI-edited documents remain unmeasurable in aggregate." That candor deserves credit, and the problem belongs to the whole field. A real statement with one altered balance has genuine structure, so a buyer who worries most about that case should weight the bake-off toward it, whichever vendor is on the table.


If none of these describe you, staying is a reasonable answer. A US lender that values network signals, uses the cash-flow insights, and has already tuned custom signals in the Decision Engine would give up a lot by switching.

## The list, in order of fit


### 1. Sphinx — Best for compliance teams that want the document check and the L1 case work done together


Sphinx sells AI compliance analysts that log into the tools a team already uses and work KYC, KYB and AML cases. Doc Fraud is one agent inside that workflow and also a standalone check. It reads a file through six signals: production method, timestamp trail, issuer matching, consistency, model artifacts and recycled patterns, and it can show what an edited field said before the edit. Sphinx reports a 94.3 percent correct verdict rate. Around the file, its[analysts](https://sphinxhq.com/products/ai-agents) prepare the evidence, apply your SOPs, and produce a traceable recommendation; your team retains final approval. Doc Fraud costs $0.45 per document with no seats, and the wider analyst product is a platform fee plus usage tiers scoped to your volumes. It suits KYB-heavy fintechs and banks. The honest limit: Sphinx offers no credit or cash-flow underwriting, does not verify faces or bank connections, and its 1M documents processed is a smaller corpus than some vendors here publish.


### 2. Resistant AI — Best for mixed, multi-country document intake


Resistant AI checks any PDF or image in more than 500 ways in under 20 seconds, and returns a Trusted, Warning or High Risk verdict with supporting evidence. Its engine is trained on more than 200 million documents, compares submissions against each other to surface serial fraud, and works in any language because it looks at how a file was built. The company also sells AML transaction monitoring. It suits risk teams at banks, payment platforms and marketplaces whose documents vary too much for type-specific models. The honest limit follows from the design: a tool that does not read what a document says leaves content logic, such as whether income figures reconcile across a file, to another system, and the investigation after the verdict stays with your team.


### 3. Ocrolus — Best for US lenders that also need extracted financial data


Ocrolus turns bank statements, pay stubs and tax documents into structured data for lending decisions, with human reviewers resolving edge cases. Its Detect product scores authenticity and returns high, medium or low risk outcomes with reason codes. Since October 2026, Detect's document forensics run on Resistant AI's engine, alongside Ocrolus's own checks on document content. It suits lenders that want data and fraud signals from one vendor, which is the closest like-for-like if Inscribe's credit features are what you value. The honest limit: its center of gravity is lending, so a compliance team may not use most of it. And because of the integration, testing Ocrolus and Resistant AI side by side does not give you two independent forensic opinions.


### 4. Fortiro — Best for income and financial documents with strict retention needs


Fortiro, headquartered in Australia and founded in 2021, checks payslips, bank statements, tax documents and invoices in around 30 seconds. It runs content, visual, metadata and forensic checks with configurable rules, and its Investigator view overlays the fraud indicators on the page. It states that it does not store customer documents beyond the initial processing period, which speaks directly to the data question above. It suits lenders and insurers that also want automated income verification. The honest limit: pricing comes through a form and an annual subscription, and a buyer leaving a network-based product should ask how a no-retention design handles repeat templates across submissions.


### 5. Doxis AI.dp — Best for enterprises wanting capture, extraction and fraud screening in one platform


Doxis AI.dp is the document processing platform formerly known as Klippa DocHorizon. SER Group announced its acquisition of Klippa in March 2025 and launched AI.dp that November. Its fraud component covers metadata and EXIF analysis, copy-move and pixel forensics, PDF modification and font checks, duplicates, and generative AI detection, with a 0 to 1 risk score on each check. It also runs two-way and three-way invoice matching. It suits operations and finance teams with broad document flows. The honest limit: fraud is one step inside a processing platform. Its documentation says the generative AI check works at page level and above rather than on specific elements, and Word and Excel files get no fraud analysis.


### 6. VerifyPDF — Best for small teams that want a self-serve check today


VerifyPDF publishes its prices, which is rare in this category. Basic costs $15 a month billed annually for 150 verifications and one user. Professional costs $79 a month billed annually for 1,000 verifications, a REST API and unlimited users, and every plan starts with a 15-day free trial. Checks typically take about 5 seconds, covering metadata, document structure, content streams and traces of known editors, and flagged files return a list of indicators. It suits teams with modest volume and no appetite for a procurement process. The honest limit comes from that focus: it answers whether a file looks tampered with, so application-level reasoning and case work stay with you, and the Basic plan has no API.


## How to choose without sitting through six demos


Start by writing down, in one sentence, why you are looking. The answer rules out most of this list before anyone gets on a call. Then work through these checks.


1. Pull a pack of documents your team has already decided, including confirmed edits of genuine files and your hardest non-US or corporate documents, and run the same pack through each finalist.[Sphinx's free playground](https://sphinxhq.com/products/doc-fraud) and VerifyPDF's trial let you start without a sales call.
2. Compare catch rates at the same flag rate. A tool that catches more by flagging twice as many files has only moved the work.
3. Time the minutes after the flag. If most of the case still happens elsewhere, a faster verdict changes little.
4. Ask every vendor, Sphinx included, the same four data questions: how long files are kept, whether they train models, whether they inform other customers' results, and what survives termination.
5. Ask whose engine is underneath. A product's name and its forensic model can come from different companies.
6. List what you would lose. Backtested custom signals, cash-flow insights and[cross-submission reuse detection](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/serial-document-reuse-detection) all take work to rebuild.


Keep the categories straight as well.[Document verification and document fraud detection](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/document-verification-vs-document-fraud-detection) answer different questions, so an identity verification vendor is a complement to Inscribe and rarely a substitute. Deloitte's Center for Financial Services predicts[generative AI could push US fraud losses to $40 billion by 2027](https://www.deloitte.com/us/en/insights/industry/financial-services/deepfake-banking-fraud-risk-on-the-rise.html) , and a shortlist built on the wrong category will not help with that number.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### What are the main alternatives to Inscribe?


The main Inscribe alternatives are Sphinx for compliance teams that want document checks and L1 case work together, Resistant AI for multi-country forensics, Ocrolus for US lenders that need extracted data, Fortiro for income documents with strict retention needs, Doxis AI.dp for enterprise document processing, and VerifyPDF for small self-serve teams. Each fits a different need, so start from yours.


### Does Inscribe have AI agents or AI analysts?


Yes. Inscribe announced AI Risk Agents and an AI Fraud Analyst in 2024, and now describes itself as an agentic document fraud platform with an in-product Assistant. Its published scope centers on reasoning across the documents in an application and researching the people and businesses behind them.


### How much does Inscribe cost?


Inscribe does not publish prices. It offers Base and Premium plans with custom pricing based on document volume and features, plus a complimentary four-week pilot on your own documents. Expect a sales conversation before you get a figure.


### Is Resistant AI or Inscribe better for document fraud?


They are built differently, so the answer depends on your files. Resistant AI looks at how a document was constructed and works on any document type and language, while Inscribe also reads content and reasons across an application, with a focus on US financial documents. Run the same pack of your own documents through both at a matched flag rate.


### Can an identity verification tool replace Inscribe?


Rarely. Identity verification confirms that a person matches a government ID, usually with a selfie, while Inscribe examines bank statements, pay stubs and other submitted files for tampering. Many teams need both, because a verified person can still submit an edited statement.
